items.body:
Tribal trance techno pioneers PWOG yield a 1st reissue of their debut album since ’93, replete with all tracks from the CD edition on vinyl. RIYL Zoviet*France, Muslimgauze, Mappa Mundi.

A real one for yoghurt weavers and armchair psychonauts, ‘Ov Biospheres And Sacred Grooves’ arrived in ’92 with a broadening and refinement of styles first spied on Psychick Warriors of Gaia’s propulsive, eponymous ’89 entry. Its maiden relaunch now christens Forever Records, a sub-division of Delsin focussed on classic album formats, with an exemplar of early ‘90s ambient techno LP interzones, surely paralleling the UK’s AI movement and characteristic of the way prevailing Euro DIY tape scenes - industrial, ambient, experimental - morphed into techno-trance and house mutations at the cusp of a new decade and era. 

The eight-track LP effectively contains the seeds of trance music as much as modern ambient club in its rangy drive between expansive, linear structures and turns toward downbeat and deep house, all of which were roughly part of the same, strange family during that pivotal period. Of course, the notion of “trance” would be codified, commercialised over the next decade, but in PWOG’s hands the sound is wide open and better defined by its sense of romance and an hypnotic immersion that patently endures for shine-eyed retro-futurists and those able to squint ears, hear the bridges between styles. 

A case in point is ‘The Challenge’, which best resembles their cult debut EP, but with a taut aerodynamic akin early Plastikman in Pt. I, but shores up in far trippier realms on a Pt. II that better reflects the rest of the LP. Between the sloshing tribalist rhythms of ‘Linkage’, the 11 min transition from nocturnal dread to buoyant 107BPM ambient house ‘The Tides (They Turn)’, or ultimate dip into warmest Balearic/Goan waters on ‘The Key (Version)’ and gently febrile ambient closer ‘New Edge Mantra’, they display how industrial, house, and ambient were all on the same page, with the same purpose that would be recognised by likeminded aerobic mystics who can join the dots.

items.body:
Lebanese vocalist Sandy Chamoun's second solo album is inspired by Sardinian polyphonic folk music the Arab ecstatic forms, modernized by synths from her SANAM and Ghadr collaborator Anthony Sayhoun and percussion from Ali Hout.

If you caught either of those heavy SANAM albums - but especially 2023's 'Aykathani Malakon' - then you'll already be familiar with Chamoun's voice, that carries the Beirut-baed band's hallucinogenic blend of folk, free jazz and acid rock. On her own, however, Chamoun gives her voice even more room to breathe, following loose historical threads to re-interpret concepts that surge through her music. The album's title means "the sound of tears" and it directly addresses the war and genocide in the Levant; Chamoun looks to tarab, an intensely emotional song form that was the first performance style she learned, to guide her through the darkness. And the influence of cantu a tenòre, a four voice polyphonic folk style that's sung in rounds, emerges on the edges. Chamoun had initially planned to journey through Lebanon writing cantu a tenòre-influenced songs that celebrated humanity's victory over nature, but as the situation deepened, the material evolved.

The two forms collide in surprising ways, though. On opening track 'Khafiy خفي', Chamoun's voice is sculpted by AutoTune and placed into an ecstatic clearing, accompanied only by slow-motion drums and scraping resonances. But on the brilliant 'Shahed شاهد', her tarab folk song dissolves mid-way through into the ether, the syncopated percussion turning into 4/4 claps and a circle of voices emerging, met eventually by Sayhoun's microtonally-tuned modular bleeps. It's music that can't help but affect the body entirely: just listen to the lulling 'Ward W Shok ورد و شوك' or the operatic extended outro 'Ataba عتابا' that runs into a moving half-sung voice note.

items.body:
On his first solo album, Paris-based Iranian artist Cinna Peyghamy (who's worked alongside Saint Abdullah & Eomac, David August, Azu Tiwaline and O.M. Theorem) plugs into a Persia that exists in only his heart by moving far beyond its boundaries, playing impossible tombak and setar sequences and disrupting them with uncanny modular processes.

Peyghamy has been working on 'Music for Tombak and Synth' since 2019, when his master's thesis research into contact microphones led him to consider sound design as a way to explore his Persian roots. He'd been working as a producer and a performer in parallel for years but has rarely unified his various approaches on record: 'Music for Tombak & Synth' gave him the opportunity to expand on the "performance-ready setup" he'd been working on with tombak and a modular system for the last few years and simultaneously examine his cultural heritage, the Iran he'd experienced via his family despite being an exile. He sees each of the album's eight compositions as deeply personal "keepsakes" that anchor the material in lived experiences, but it also never sounds nostalgic. Far from it, in fact; Peyghamy's layered rhythms and glassy synths are jarringly futuristic, sounding closer to Mohammad Reza Mortazavi's elasticated experiments, or even Sote's modernist folk reboot 'Parallel Persia'.

He's loath to describe the material as "electroacoustic" and we can hear why. The rhythms and indeed some of the melodic elements are undoubtedly rooted in acoustic instruments, but Peyghamy pulls the sounds up by their stalks, re-planting them in unfamiliar soil. And the process, while roughly the same for each composition, often yields very different results. Opener 'Mutosy' materializes in a dubwise space, coating its tombak rhythms in comb-filtered, ping-ponging reverberations that wouldn't sound out of place on a Monolake record and adding plodding bass that seems to work against the high-end rhythms, creating an unsettling clockwork effect. 'Zur زور' meanwhile sounds ritualistic in comparison, meeting its stirring rhythms in a wide open outdoor space, with metallic, xenharmonic melodies sounding like alien flutes or mechanical bird calls in the distance. Setar twangs slow dance with stuttering modular belches on the brilliant 'La Nesque', creating another dimension for Peyghamy to explore, and on the album's thematic centerpiece 'Dar Shab در شب', the artist's dad (who also took the album's evocative cover photo) appears, reciting a poem from iconic Iranian poet, writer and journalist Ahmad Shamlou over Peyghamy jr's reverberant soundscape. Another winner for Nicolas Jaar's Other People imprint.

DINTE dip into a rich archival pot of 1930’s-1950’s rural Greek demotika, a style of folksong rooted in the Byzantine era and practised between Greece and its diaspora.

Timeless themes of love, death, matrimony, nature and whatever is the Greek word for “the craic”, spur the singers on board to a range of keening laments of the slower Syrtos style, and ecstatic folk dance of the Pidiktos mode, in time-honoured style across ‘Curse You, Foreign Lands’.

While those themes may only be literally understood by Greek speakers, the songs’ passionately emotive delivery transcends tongues, variously mesmerising on the swaying, forlorn romance of Georgia Vasilopoulou, and male/female vocal in the heady helix of Nikolaos Chalkias’ ‘Σταφύλι μοσχοστάφυλο’, which kinda reminds us of Thai molam, or instrumentally emoting as on two standouts by Vaios Malliaras, while saving a drum and horn-led gem for Kostas Zografos’ ‘Ανάπλι στο βουλευτικό’.

Coinciding with Masami Akita’s UK shows of ’26, a reminder of his early, groundbreaking prowess surfaces in remastered edition of his ’85 tape, recorded at the Merz-bau studio.

Originally dispensed on his ZSF Produkt label as ‘Nil Vagina Mail-Action’, the hour long session is all assembled from his early analogue set-up and newly cleft in five parts hungry to demolish the senses.  Not a live performance, but a ‘Life Performance’, signature torrents of atonality are punctuated with blasts of what we suspect to be intercepted radio frequencies, the smashing sounds of a Greek wedding, and frankly fuck knows whatever else he tosses in the pot. It’s Merzbow, you know what you’re getting, and it pays hard on delivery.

Low-key cult Japanese house entity Shin Watanabe trades in pure, redlit deep house sleaze on a substantial debut payload for L.I.E.S.

‘Red Zone-Ethos Mama Trax’ arrives in the wake of Watanabe’s introductory ‘Album 1986’ (Hot Street Records, 2025) with a sureshot affirmation of his greazy steez up-to-the-hilt on 13 ‘floor-ready jams. The spectres of earliest Chi and NYC house are summoned with strong attention to the sound’s subtle variegation and fine grasp of its raw but classy hallmarks, or more simply what makes it endure in the dance floor’s collective imagination.

Tune to tune he pinpoints the sound coming into its own from a blend of prevailing disco, industrial, soul and synth-pop touchstones, and with particular emphasis on its sinuous, psychosexual thirst/thrust. Shake  stick and you’ll hit an ace anywhere across the set, from the haughty stride and belting vox of pt. VI thru the sexy Lynchian chords of pt. III, to DJ Pierre-esque percolations in pt. I, a Burrell Brothers-like pt. II, the body-floatigb warehouse sassy of pt. VII, and Virgo Fpur styles on pt. X.

items.body:
Enigmatic producer Soda Plains returns with his first solo set in four years; 'Rouveau Niche' is a mixed bag, a handful of saturated beatless themes and taut, trancey dancefloor workouts that the London-based producer disturbs with powdery distortion.

Last time we heard from Alexis Chan, he was working side-by-side with young singer/producer Rachel Lu, aka LVRA, designing instruments and re-imagining pop forms on 2025's 'Fortress'. And not long before that, he'd launched his New Triple Gold imprint with 'Living With Elvis', a brief rave diversion that recycled all yer classic '92 aesthetics and treated 'em to a fresh lick of paint. He's back on firmer ground with 'Rouveau Niche' though, wading through murkier waters before he even trips over a beat. Opener 'Dirge' is fittingly titled, crushing its shrill notes with industrial-grade distortion before 'New Job' plays like a discarded witch house memory. 

It's only when we hit 'Blister' that Chan's slippery, precision-engineered rhythms make an appearance, rasping past Koreless-style risers and soft focus bass. And on 'If the Red Stops Redding', although the kicks and hats disappear, there's an outline of grime beneath the acidic squelches, brassy womps and overpowering Metal Zone crunchiness. In fact, Chan doesn't attempt to throw any more percussion in until the final track, 'Gawain's Gaiwan', a slow medieval romp that pairs its videogame-strength FM string fanfare with a rattling, bitcrushed march to the chopping block.

items.body:
Good Morning Tapes back with a new album of lushest New Age sound-bathing x emotionally gooey trip hop from Andro Gogibedashvili aka Saphileaum, delivered in a mode that’s highly tipped for anyone on the line from Enigma to All Saints, from a.s.o to Boards of Canada.

Saphileaum has spent the past decade in passage between notable houses of atmospheric sorcery - Mule Musiq, Not Not Fun, Slow Life, Constellation Tatsu - and of course Good Morning Tapes, who now host their 3rd meeting, ‘Heavenly Hills’. A definitive chapter in his ten year saga, it is flush with symphonic strings and sky born keys, breezily urged by percussion that straddles chill out and folk zones. That said there’s also a Balearic - or should that be Black Sea? - appeal to its title tune, that lingers in the glistening wake of ‘Your Grace’, to the shimmering breaks of a parting piece ‘Alarko (Cosmic Eagle)’, falling into the space between Boards of Canada's cult-inspired hauntological nostalgia and Shackleton's hallowed ethno-dub.

“The tracks in the album were written with the inspiration of the kingdom of Shambhala in the Himalayas. I'm deeply fascinated and touched by it. Even the album title, holds the idea of its Heavenly nature and the tracks are like individual, elemental parts of it. The album is not a journey into Shambhala, but rather a play and a dance with its energy, image and presence in my world. Alarko (Cosmic Eagle) is dedicated to my grandfather, Temur Tsiklauri, and I dedicate the whole album to my country Georgia, which I deeply love.”

The eternal sunrise of late ’80s / early ’90s Goa dance & European proto-trance guides Alexis Le Tan & Joakim’s cult duo on their by-now trademarked style of chopped & screwed x Mediterranean drug chug hypno-bullets, pulling a broad range of source material into their own world of hazed offbeat grooves and arps with a rare je ne sais quoi that’s made their catalogue a proper cult property, fulfilling a need for this type of aerobic mysticism on modern dancefloors.

As with their slew of Good Morning Tapes mixes and LPs it’s all arranged with a slick, sick, effortless aerodynamic, glyding between the likes of their subcontinental-slanted rework of fellow French psych-o-nauts Vox Populi!, and the remix for Die Orangen that really placed them on the map back in 2019. It’s never hurried, always zoned-in, flowing with a careful attention to the good of your trip and heavy as you like.

The frisson is real!

items.body:
Dark Entries salvage from tape obscurity choice morsels of ’91-’93 industrial x dark ambient by Nagamatzu’s Stephen Jarvis as Pure Motorised Instinct, all swooning, grandiose gothic synths and doom-leaden drums akin to Coil’s Hellraiser score.

“Pure Motorised Instinct drives over to Dark Entries with At Last I’m Leaving the Earth, an LP of industrial-tinged ambient and new age. When legendary industrial outfit Nagamatzu went dormant in 1991, band member Stephen Jarvis moved forward with Pure Motorised Instinct, a name he pulled from a line in George Romero’s Dawn of the Dead. Throughout two cassette albums – 1991’s Between Intimacy and Elsewhere, and 1993’s Everything Is True – Jarvis pushed the Nagamatzu spirit in new directions. At Last I’m Leaving the Earth collects 9 tracks from this era, which are appearing on vinyl for the first time, along with 3 additional tracks on a bonus CD. The material here sits between the brooding and the optimistic, the claustrophobic and the soporific. Jarvis’s digital synths are pushed so far into tape-scuffed terrain that they talk and squawk analog-like, scurrying with vibrant curiosity. The late-night vibes peak on pieces like “Vincent V,” with its reverb-drenched digital drum machines, or “Geek,” which taps into a wide-eyed proto-vaporwave zone. At Last I’m Leaving the Earth is Black Lodge ambient for the empty set.”

items.body:
Ditching the free jazz, at least for a spell, sax prodigy Zoh Amba follows their blistering deployments for Smalltown and Tzadik and collaborations with Wobbly, Chris Corsano and Bill Orcutt with an album of fragile indie Americana. Unexpected, for sure, but welcome - RIYL 'Eureka'-mode Jim O'Rourke, early Joanna Newsom, Bonnie 'Prince' Billy or Bill Callahan.

Still in their mid-20s, Amba has already lived a lifetime on the US improv scene, releasing so many records in the space of the last half-decade that it's easy to understand why they needed some downtime. The story goes that they were back in their hometown of Kingsport, Tennessee - the birthplace of horror legend Nick Castle, who played Michael Myers in the first 'Halloween' - when they were inspired to drop their horn and tinker with their old acoustic guitar, the first instrument they learned to play, way back when. The instrument itself isn't really the most unexpected thing about 'Eyes Full', though, most surprising is the way Amba approaches it. Although they're a seasoned free improv fixture, there's none of the expected aesthetics on show here; quite the opposite, in fact, the album sounds as if it's barely aware that Albert Ayler existed, instead spying classic Appalachian folk, Nashville alt-country and headsy indie-rock for its creative Cliff's Notes. 

Listen in carefully though and you'll be able to identify the same eccentric energy that coursed through last year's excellent 'Sun'. Amba's voice is immediately a draw, molded into a drawl of elongated vowels and half-tuned syllables that sounds as if it's locked into a lineage that you can easily trace back to Alan Lomax's American folk field recordings. And their performance on the guitar seems to work to accent that distinct phrasing, indebted to John Fahey and his acolytes in a way, but also purposefully rough around the edges, punk-y, even. There's something about the way Amba is able to stab at the strings and turn the guitar into a percussive instrument for a second before lurching it back to melody that betrays their background. And their choice of collaborators is also key: they're backed up on 'Eyes Full' by drummer Jim White and their bestie Kevin Hyland on electric guitar, and the songs evolved through session after session of rehearsals. 

So there's a tightness here that's somehow shaped into pop that's ragged enough to feel fresh, vital and different. Lead single 'Another Time' will help you understand what planet they're on, with Amba's tactile strums and throaty intimacies wrapped casually around their collaborators' chic scaffolding. "In another lifetime, I take you to the sea," they half-screech. "I show you honey, how sweet that soul's meant to be." And on 'Southern Soil', they reflect on the history of small town, working class folk music in America, taking the lead with an acrobatic vocal performance that sounds as if it belongs in church. Even if you're missing the old Amba, there's a glimmer of improv running through 'Child You'll See' just for the heads, when their jangling guitar is swallowed by filthy reverb trails and supplanted by drones and pained sax wails. Very nice.

items.body:
John Howes’ crucial pivot to the cult Paperclip Minimiser generates unique fractal chain reactions on a strong 12” for Blank Mind - RIYL Carrier, Sasu Ripatti, Purelink.

As heard on the project’s eponymous, sought-after ’22 debut and its recent follow-up for Peak Oil, sound designer/arranger Howes doesn’t just pay lip service to notions of electronic futurism; he enacts it from the ground up with custom-built software, a vivid imagination, and deep R&D. In Howes hands electronic material is made extremely malleable and unusually organic, arranging elemental vapours and fleeting drums in loosey goosey polymetrics that offer dancing bodies or minds myriad options for movement. Its a type of synaesthetic sound that has clearly snagged the senses of those keenly observing mutations of the dub tech sound, and here presented at its most pliable, plonging and spongiform - something to get the ear’s teeth right into.

Said it before and will again; Paperclip Minimiser’s sound really comes into its own with proper amplification, where his finely spaced-out frequencies and their fluid interaction really comes into play. Up top ‘TT A1’ flexes over 8 mins of hypnotic club levitation where drums barely touch the ‘floor, held in sublime suspense with a grasp of deferred gratification that has become his calling card, whilst ‘TT A2’ expresses a more romantic, hair-kissing lustre in its opalescent shimmer and sway. B-side ‘TT B1’ feels to beautifully gels, merges the preceding aesthetics in headiest form; rhythms zipping off into infinite dub ether of lushly anaesthetic pads with an ingenious tongue-and-toe-tip proprioception that leaves us swooning. 

Tip!

Gast on the mixing desk. 

It’s not hard to hear Nicolini’s input on Devon Rexi surface across the album, from its spicy sirens and animated idents to the deftness of his wrong-footing grooves. It’s all there in centrepiece ‘Bottle J’, where steppas bass collides hip-shot sampler stabs and autotune, and likewise in ‘Girma Come In My Light’, but zipped up on a deep south rap downstroke. He’s also prone to hybridise gothic rap bells with grimy soca drums on ‘Rompe Mi Cabeza’, and fuse singeli with flamenco on ‘BBY Spoon’, or go like haywire digickal steppas on ‘Deep Tissue Killa Riddim’, all primed to send a dance hectic.

items.body:
Eric Dolphy’s landmark LP of the same title, overhauled with typical instruments, and atypical electronics (sine waves, contact mike, no-input mixing board, and computer), plus inventive spirit, by leading Japanese improvisor Otomo Yoshihide, and ensemble.

“Though Dolphy should not be considered an avant-garde musician by the term's most common definitions, most interpretations of Out To Lunch have been done by players working squarely in that area. So it is with this album, the most ambitious in its recreation of the five-tune disc (with one original added to the final "Straight Up and Down, extending the piece to almost thirty minutes). All five compositions from the original quintet LP are revisited in the same order, the record sleeve even duplicates the old album jacket, down to the typeface and black-and-blue color scheme, although a photo taken by Daidō Moriyama inside Tokyo's massive (and massively busy) Shinjuku railway station replaces the Dolphy's album's enigmatic "Will Be Back" sign, whose clock hands indicated no conventional time of expected return.

Otomo Yoshihide first came to international prominence in the 1990s as the leader of the experimental rock group Ground Zero, and has since worked in a variety of contexts, ranging from free improvisation to noise, jazz, avant-garde and contemporary classical. The always surprising and sometimes confounding turntablist, sound artist, onkyo improviser and now avant jazzer heading up a 15-piece aggregation of Japanese and European experimentalists. Who better to grapple with Dolphy's legacy -- so idiosyncratic in its day and yet so influential to creative improvisers who followed -- than a musician with his own singular take on how sounds can be organized in the jazz realm over 40 years later and half a world away? In other words don't expect the conventional from Otomo any more than you would from Dolphy himself. That's not to say that recognizable themes ("Hat and Beard," "Out to Lunch," "Straight Up and Down") don't appear, or that individual players -- including Alfred Harth on bass clarinet bursting into the mix and leaping across the instrument's tonal range in a way that recalls the master himself -- don't carry forward echoes from the past in the spirit of a sincere and heartfelt homage.

However, a good deal of the time all bets are off; in addition to the usual brass, reeds, bass, and drums (and of course a bit of vibraphone, here played by Takara Kumiko in far less prominent role than that of Bobby Hutcherson) are such sonic paraphernalia as sine waves, contact mike, no-input mixing board, and, of course, "computer." (Otomo himself plays skronky electric guitar.) From composition to composition and even during episodes within compositions, the band takes radically different approaches. There are blasts of free jazz energy not too far removed from the Peter Brötzmann Tentet, an impression reinforced by the presence of spluttering wildman Mats Gustafsson on baritone sax. Not surprisingly and often in contrast with the Dolphy original, the music is dense and filled to overflowing with sounds -- sometimes due to fundamental reworkings in structure rather than just the larger size of the ensemble. The middle section of "Something Sweet, Something Tender" somewhat belies the original's title with elongated howls and cries from the horns over slo-mo bass, drums, and electronic noise poised somewhere between dirge and drone, and the sudden explosion of punk-ish rock energy in the following "Gazzelloni" is a startling contrast.

At times, the feeling is that of listening to the original Out To Lunch while a séance is going on to contact Dolphy's ghost, with supernatural sounds swirling around the stereo. The effect is disconcerting, as is the post-apocalyptic cloud hanging over the arrangements, but it makes the effort more than an unnecessary tribute album. Instead, Dolphy is transported into the 21st Century and allowed to romp through modern developments in music. An inspiring concept and an album that will stretch the boundaries of anyone who comes into contact with it.”

items.body:
New LP from Italo-Vietnamese Brussels-based artist Radio Hito via Meakusma & Bologna label Maple Death - "a ten-sequence song cycle for voice and MIDI soundfonts adapted from the 2021 book by French poet Claude Royet-Journoud"

"Certain paths necessitate and call for one singular long sequence in order to arrive at a fully formed conversation or reasoning. Nothing seems to broadcast it more clearly than the trajectory Brussels based Italo-Vietnamese artist Nguyễn Zen Mỹ embarked on during the last decade as Radio Hito.

After a string of highly cherished and sought out tape releases, Radio Hito’s new album ‘L’uso e gli attributi del cuore’, co-released by Maple Death & Meakusma, unfolds with devastating clarity, a profound balance of depth, minimalism and emotional grounding. A ten-sequence song cycle for voice and MIDI soundfonts adapted from the 2021 book by French poet Claude Royet-Journoud.

Written and recorded between January 2023 and August 2025, the cycle evolved through nearly 80 live performances from Galicia to Kazakhstan before arriving at its recorded form. Set to an Italian libretto adapted from Royet-Journoud’s text ‘L'usage et les attributs du cœur’ (POL, 2021), the work revisits the tradition of the 19th-century Lied — art song built on existing poetry— transposed into a radically economical contemporary setting: voice and Casio CTK workstations.

"I was interested by this incompleteness CRJ mentions - by the ‘suspension’ of meaning questioning readability and intelligibility. I ‘resisted’ to CRJ’s texts since I met him and got to know his work. […] It seems to me that when playing the songs, I submit an object to be completed by the audience."

Radio Hito’s distinctive approach to setting poetry to music — spare arrangements, strophic repetition, and a voice suspended between recital, fm transmission and canzone — creates a language of its own, reaching new heights on ‘L’uso e gli attributi del cuore’, songs that are formally rigorous, emotionally restrained, and shaped by the discipline of sustained live performance, interlocking into a coherent cycle.

Rather than illustrating the poem, Radio Hito approaches it as a space of suspension. Royet-Journoud described poetry as a “profession of ignorance” where meaning remains incomplete; these songs extend that trembling state, allowing repetition, digital timbre, and restraint to hold the text open.

Often misread as minimal synth or romantic chanson, Radio Hito’s practice is rooted instead in the lineage of the art song and song cycle: open structures, close attention to language, and a live performance economy that pushes the voice at the heart of the stage. The choice of accessible keyboard workstations — light, portable, and embedded in contemporary popular culture — replaces the historical piano.

Radio Hito creates fantastical, mirage-like songs, intimate yet elusive. Her music is forlorn chanson for the digital age; bringing her haunting and beautiful vocalisations into conversation with MIDI soundfonts and humble-yet-deep casio compositions. Music that strides for simplicity, yet lands miraculously within an entire new universe, a uniqueness achieved from like-minded spirits such as Ghedalia Tazartès, Savina Yannatou & Lena Platonos, Dorothy Carter, cycles that trickle down into estuaries."

items.body:
A second pressing of last year’s gorgeous fourth and final album from Old Saw, the American Primitive project of Tongue Depressor's Henry Birdsey, riffing on the classic Takoma paradigm with additional ferric washes and layered instrumental drones, huge recommendation if yr into Bruce Langhorne’s ‘The Hired Hand’ or classic work by Daniel Lanois, Laraaji, Pelt, Stars Of The Lid, State River Widening.

'The Wringing Cloth' is Birdsey’s fourth and final Old Saw outing, and ironically it’s also the one that has garnered most amount of critical and commercial success. Old Saw’s shimmering, drone-heavy soundscapes were recorded on 1/4" tape at various locations in New England over the last few years and are once again paired with evocative black and white imagery from photographer Dylan Hausthor, whose landscapes somehow perfectly capture the timeless, widescreen appeal of the music inside.

Birdsey's pedal, lap steel and resonator are at the core of each track, but the album also features Old Saw’s usual personnel; Harper Reed on nylon string guitar and banjo, Ira Dorset on fiddle and bowed strings, Ann Rowlis on reed organ and harmonium, Jim Cutler on telecaster, Addison Starkweather-Price on bass, and Peter Catchpole on metal objects and power hammer. That lap steel lends the music its stylistic anchor, taking us through decades of American folk before gently fraying at the edges. Birdsey's application of classical minimalism - the themes that surge through his work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor - is still somehow present here, especially as the record pulls into its second side and the shimmering country-fied atmosphere is pierced with bell-like sounds, but the overall mood and flavour of the record is distinctly easy on the ear and timeless in its appeal.

As the label put it, “What has always been uncanny about this music is that it arrives in a state at once familiar and obscured, like a memory weighed down with sensory information but no identifying details to place it. The Wringing Cloth walks off further into that geographical dream without time or language, until it’s just a speck of light….”

items.body:
Dead strong and curious rhythmic bliss on that distinctive tip shared with SND/Mark Fell, Gábor Lázár, goat (JP), Beatrice Dillon and Eli Keszler, with some added jazzwise sauce.

Following up 2024's Fibonacci-friendly 'Yucca', producer Church Andrews and percussionist Matt Davies return with an ear-bending set of skewed thizzlers. Inspired by Terry Riley, John Coltrane and Dilla, they developed their style by jamming with a keyboard and drum kit, mimicking DAW-brained fractal generated biz until they reached the level of Japanese titans goat (JP), where you can hardly tell whether you're listening to a group of humans or a Max/MSP patch loaded up with algorithms. 

They continue to challenge themselves on 'Tilt', complicating the rhythms even further and introducing the kind of chiming microtonalities you'd expect to hear on any number of Aleksi Perälä’s thousands of releases. Loosen yr mind into the groove and everything begins to make sense; after the clockwork funk of the Gábor Lázár-alike lead single 'Yokai', the album shifts into drive with 'Debris', reaching a jazzy apex on the discordant (and surprisingly cinematic) standout 'Noir'. We're sure you're tired of hearing the word "microtonal" at this point, but there's no denying the charms of a good xenharmonic scale when it's deployed so expertly.

Real good.

London’s soul positive festival-turned-family, GALA hail a decade of community action with 15 cuts spanning Charlie Dark’s spoken word to Marcellus Pittman’s choice deep house, soca-techno from Amaliah, and Yu Su’s dreamy garage-house glyder...

"Ten Years of GALA is both an archive and a horizon: a reflection on where GALA has come from, and a signal of what lies ahead. Founded in 2016 as a one-day gathering in South London, GALA has grown into a global point of reference for dancers, artists and collectives drawn together by a shared commitment to independence, collaboration and underground music culture. Rather than charting success through scale alone, the festival has consistently prioritised integrity, community and musical curiosity – values that underpin this release.

Spanning fifteen tracks, Ten Years of GALA unfolds as a considered journey. It opens with an intimate spoken contribution from Charlie Dark, grounding the compilation firmly in GALA’s home of Peckham before gradually expanding outward into fuller, club-focused terrain. From there, the record moves between moods and tempos, tracing a path from reflective moments into the physical language of the dancefloor.

The compilation brings together longtime friends of the festival alongside newer voices drawn into its orbit in recent years. Each artist contributes a distinct perspective, but collectively the tracks form a coherent portrait – not of a single sound, but of a shared ethos shaped over ten years of gatherings, collaborations and days spent dancing together.

Rather than a retrospective in the conventional sense, Ten Years of GALA functions as a living document. It captures fragments of past editions, scenes and relationships, while remaining firmly oriented toward the future. These are not museum pieces, but records designed to be played, shared and folded back into the spaces from which they came. Together, the compilation holds a piece of GALA’s first decade – not as a closed chapter, but as a foundation for what comes next."

items.body:
Donato Dozzy and Neel's critically lauded 2012 opus is re-pressed for 2026, highlighting just how influential it's been in the years since,

If you're into psychedelic, trance-inducing minimal techno, then you've probably come across Voices from the Lake already. If not, then prepare yerself for an interface with yr new favorite album. Released over a decade ago, the record made an immediate connection with clubgoers searching for a lysergic alternative to minimal's booming, avoidant monotony. Dozzy and Neel approach their tracks with enviable restraint: kick drums are present on the self-titled album, but forced into submission, not dominating the tracks but occasionally adding punctuation to their whirling structures. The key to each segment - which run into each other to form a longform heat haze of abstract percussion and offworld sound effects - isn't the drums exactly, but the mood the two Italian veterans are able to extract using only the most spartan ingredients.

The elements are familiar - cycling melodic phrases, distant pads, unstable rhythms - but the way Dozzy and Neel assemble them feels human and connected. On 'Iyo' there's barely a chance for the track to develop into a proper banger; all tension, no release. Elsewhere on 'Manuvex' the kick is softened into a damp thud, left to underpin shivery Porter Ricks-esque glitches and peculiar, dissonant synthetic elements that breathe with rare humanity. With the shortest track weighing in at a generous seven and a half minutes, and the longest hitting 16, it's an epic that's not afraid of simmering in its own juices until it's fully cooked. Bit of a classic?

Bristol’s quietly revelatory Tara Clerkin Trio usher a magnificent new 30 minute mini album of folk-jazz and classical-downbeat chamber music x dreampop with their return trip for London’s World of Echo, hugely tipped if yr into Laika, Pram, Broadcast, Hydroplane, A.R. Kane, Portishead, Laila Sakini.

Effortless and transcendent, Tara Clerkin Trio unpick and rethread myriad 90’s DIY tropes on an undeniably genius new mini album that takes the brittle, asymmetric pop of Pram, Stereolab’s orchestral arrangements, A.R. Kane’s penchant for straight looped-Amen-dreampop, and drape it with esoteric and uncomproimisingly modern chamber jazz and baroque folk baubles that are just impossible not to fall deeply in love with.

Aye that title track is an instant wonder, and shares a 90’s undercurrent with the more dubwise ‘World in Delay’, where echoes of Laika’s hybrid vibrations surface to transport us to a different time. ‘Marble Walls’, meantime, manages to remind us of both Broadcast’s ‘Tears In The Typing Pool’ and Stereolab’s 'Cybele's Reverie', all sweeping orchestral flourishes urged by a daydreamy, bubbling rhythm. 

The rest catches them in measuredly introspective mode, tidily drifting along streams of ferric hiss, rippling marimba and accordion into a hazy fantasy like Don Cherry meets A.R. Kane on the downbeat slunk of ‘Brigstow’, and folding a lute riff into loopy origami on the glorious, pastoral fade to close of ‘Once Again’. 

Stunner.

The craziest label in Detroit back with another genius, unfathomable dose of destroyed Techno x Trip Metal, caked in Motor City crud and located on the factory line somewhere between Urban Tribe, H-Fusion and Wolf Eyes​

Seven years on from his debut ‘Bloodsport’, secretive 313 artist K-6000 only jags deeper into Detroit’s scuzzy underbelly on the rough hewn rhythmic noise and atmospheric trip metal of ‘War Games’. The 6-part album surely evokes the dystopia of modern Detroit’s knackered architecture in its cranky tone and offbeat structure, but also signals the underlying soul of its entities, and the lost futures they live thru, in its textured play of psyched sax and guitar spectres meshed with sampledelic tapestry of disembodied voices. 

A record that leaves dirt under yr nails, it unfurls at its own steady pace from free jazz noise like some Wolf Eyes re-score of Robocop, into grouchy bouts of squashed beatdown psych with ruggedest drum programming comparable to KDJ, Shake and Sherard Ingram’s chops with Kemetrix on the Urban Tribe album. It descends into the sleaziest mire of Blind Pig biker bar blooz, like Captain Beefheart jamming with H-Fusion, around the mid-section, and ultimately buckles into PCP-spiked industrial funk sludge in the final stages. 

Manna for sci-fi free jazz trip metal beatdown hounds, then!

Surf Gang co-founder Harrison follows his work on MIKE and Earl Sweatshirt's 'POMPEII // UTILITY' with his first solo album, a tight set of wonky, atmospheric instrumentals that establishes him as one of rap's most reliable minimalists.

Harrison's been around for ages - he even held the camera on those Spooky Black videos back in the day - but it was only this year when his profile really spiked. Previously an almost anonymous presence alongside Evilgiane in New York City's Surf Gang collective, Harrison's work on 'POMPEII // UTILITY', an ambitious double album that he produced almost single handedly, took his name far beyond Reddit threads and YouTube credits. And the modestly titled 'Taking a walk & calling a car home' arrives only a matter of weeks later, sweeping up 10 of the beatmaker's oddest cues, collaborations with Bryce Byrd, Cajm, Earl Sweatshirt, Elipropperr, Harto Falión and TAKA and moody solo experiments that help establish his lore. On the opener, for example, the expected roll of clipped hi-hats and booming 808s never arrives; instead we're trapped in an uncanny back alley, met with saturated FM pads, ghostly moans and pulsing bass twangs.

Alba Collective's ambient/improv operative Byrd shows with an assist on 'graffititowers1&2', a squashed, Actress-like house sketch with breathy Y2K synths and London's Cajm, who we last spotted working alongside Bianca Scout, appears on 'Fieldsloop', a glitchy rumble of clicks 'n cuts percussion and booming bass. Even when Earl joins for 'officeloop with t + e', the mood never ruptures, carrying Surf Gang's most ambient ambitions into unknown territory with ratcheting foley clanks and reverberating woodwind loops. And when Virginia rapper Harto Falión breaks the silence on 'Wrong', it's with wordless chants that sound more horizontal than Harrison's comparatively upbeat kicks and snaps. It's worth holding out until the title track, six minutes of submerged, almost dubbed-out rhythms, Badalamenti keys and cryptic SFX that helps us contextualize the entire record. Whatever Harrison's doing, it's not strictly rap, that's for sure.

YOUTH return with a second dose of inexorable House pressure from Paul Bennett aka Duster Valentine, primed for DJs and dancers and a sureshot tip FFO Michael J. Blood, Todd Terry, Ron Trent, Anthony “Shake” Shakir, DJ Sprinkles…

Aye it’s another haul of hard hitting gems pressed to vinyl for the first time, a love note to formative years in the ‘80s and early ‘90s, off his chops at The Haçienda and other legendary Manchester spots. It’s a masterclass in demonstrating the flavours-within-a-theme that emerged from the Chi, 313, and NYC during that pivotal era, and which would eventually light the touch paper of a UK club revolution. 

In Duster Valentine’s hands, the sound is presented stripped to salient fundamentals, before it went commercial, ranging from sampler-knuckling garage-house stabbers thru haughty canter and plushest, pendulous grooves. He homes in hard on the exact point when hip hop and electro gave way to house in the Todd Terry-via-Pal Joey style jam ‘Getting’ Dub’, and gives a big salute to Chez N Trent’s rugged, chord-riding haughtiness via Levon Vincent in ‘Hit Me From Behind’.

‘Strobelight Honnies’ leans into the sound’s deepest ends with a perfectly weighted bassline, cold drums and sublime string tension dubbed with hypnotic elegance, where ‘The KatG Chord’ follows with shimmers of Anthony Shakir via Michael J Blood. Suffice it to say they’re all essential and bang on the dollar if you know what’s good.

100% perlers!

Comprehensive set from Merzbow & Gen P-O’s 1999 encounter, tipped for the curious masochists and those who know what they’re in for.

Birds of a feather, the UK miscreant and Japanese berserker meet on mutual, scorched earth, with Gen’s nasal whine sometimes placed inside, at others outside, Akita’s signature maelstrom. To be fair, we’re really not sure who does what instrumentally - they’re both capable of conjuring atonal mazzas - but it’s clear who does the voice at least. They sound like an evil voice in your head on a chart ready 3 min title tune, and paced higher in the mix like a cult leader heard thru a Tannoy on ‘Flowering Pain Give Space’, and treated to more Burroughsian dissection and hellish processing on ‘Source Are Rare’. Best (worst?) of all, they prowl the grinding groove of ‘Kreeme Horne’ like a brothel madam holding court at the bar, and when creeping the buckled structure of high frequency squall and junk brutalism of ‘All Beauty is Our Enemy’.

True skool Chicago house don Mark Grusane packs inch-tight jakbeat budge and hypnotic depth on a definitive 6-track statement for his label, Disctechno and FFO Traxx, Adonis, Jamal Moss

A Windy City staple who has been DJing since the early ‘90s, and producing for over 20 years, Grusane’s experienced touch is tangible on all six tracky jams of ‘A House of My Own’. It’s a low-key masterclass in finding variation within a style, working the ruddiest bass and reedy synths to the bone on the title tune, and going tripper with it on ‘Essence of Life (Afterhours Mix)’, with over-the-shoulder vocals that are removed on its brighter ‘Daytime Mix’, and replaced with weird chirrups. He brings the acid to a gnarly simmer on the cold beat track ‘Knock Knock, Who’s There’, and taps a classic vein of Chi darkroom smut in the NSFW ace ‘Love and Lust (Explicit Lyrics)’, beside the filthy buck of ‘Jack Your Ass’.

After curating beloved annual edits comps for years, Latane Hughes and Billy Scher are now making their own music with the help of producer Miles Felix.

"Look, there are a lot of DJ duos in Brooklyn. Most of them are fine. Fundido are the kind who’ve been doing the good work for 10 years. What started as euphoric, after-band free-for-alls in the front room at Baby’s All Right now takes place in increasingly bigger rooms, further afield, regulars and new faces side by side. It’s a music lover’s paradise and a responsible adult’s worst nightmare.

“Get A Grip” felt almost purpose-built for DFA: four-on-the-floor drums, a synth that maws away your inhibitions, a vocal from Emma Dufaux that closes the deal. It’s really good.

The 12” gives you four ways to hear it: the Original Mix, a Bliss Mix (less maw), and remixes from rising stars Make A Dance and Asa Tate. These guys spent a decade learning what makes people lose themselves and keep coming back. Now they’re making the tracks to match."

items.body:
The Jamaican icon's final project, 'Spatial, No Problem' took Lee "Scratch" Perry to Berlin in 2019, where he laid down a series of surreal improvisations alongside Jan St. Werner and Andi Toma's spiky electronics.

When Perry died in 2021, bands rushed to put out their collaborations with the octogenarian hero, each claiming they had his final session: was it New Age Doom's 'Lee "Scratch" Perry's Guide to the Universe' or Pete Harris and Fritz Caitlin's 'Mercy'? The real answer is that it was a project he'd made with Mouse on Mars just a couple of years earlier; St. Werner and Toma weren't quite sure how they'd made the cut (it could have been a label connection, or a prior collaboration with a friend of Perry's, they never found out) and when Perry showed up at their Paraverse studio they were in shock. "We hardly spoke about what we were doing," explains St. Werner. "We met and got going. He was laughing a lot and we laughed along. We also cooked and ate fish soup and papayas."

Perry sounds old on 'Spacial, No Problem", sure, but he sounds as eccentric as ever, free associating over Mouse On Mars's seemingly casual blend of dub, krautrock, spiritual jazz and punky noise. Maybe they were the ideal collaborators to see Perry off the earthly plane; it's not your average dub album, but Perry wasn't your average artist, either.

items.body:
Dutch techno duo Artefakt invite KMRU to assist on their third 'Collaborations' volume, improvising with the Kenyan sound artist in the studio to capture the immediacy of their exchange.

'Collaborations III' follows last year's short, sharp EP with Mayaan Nidam and its predecessor, a record of deep techno variations made alongside Sardinian producer Claudio PRC. This one's the series' most generous set so far and started life in 2023 when the trio found themselves at Pulse, a wooden cabin-cum-studio in the Brandeburg forest. This is where most of the improvisations were initially formulated and in the second session, at Artefakt's Berlin studio, they dubbed the two solo piano tracks and finished the arrangements. It's charming material, as you might imagine, that deviates from Artefakt's prior material and KMRU's noisy recent gear. Made mostly of pillowy, synth-led drones and subtle environmental sounds, it's prime gear for sinking into your surroundings to.

items.body:
Following up last year's ace 'Off The Record', Roméo Poirier works with his father, Philippe Lamiral Poirer, on a series of tracks based on his written texts, and evocative spoken word expressions that Roméo animates with suitably effervescent exotica-inspired productions.

A versatile musician, painter and filmmaker who was best known for his work in French "ambient rock" band Kat Onoma, Philippe Poirier died last year, leaving behind a deep catalog. 'Images parlées' is a touching reflection on his impact on Roméo's own artistic path that's different from anything in the younger Poirier's catalog to date. It's led by Philippe's breathy, poetic recitations that even in isolation would already be worth checking into. Roméo rises to the challenge, calling back to the glory days of French exotica - think Jean-Claude Vannier's work on Serge Gainsbourg's landmark 1971 album 'Histoire de Melody Nelson' - and infusing a medley of Hammond vamps, reverberating strings and double bass with his signature smeared glitches and subtle loops. 

What's remarkable about 'Images parlées' is how restrained it is. Recorded between 2022 and 2024, it plays like a celebration of the father and son duo's artistic connection, not a solemn, somber remembrance but trans-generational meeting place, between '70s French avant-lounge and contemporary collage. On 'En soixante et en dix-huit', Philippe's voice swerves from an almost-whisper to almost-singing as Roméo meets his energy with moody Gallic organs and Moog wails that he cuts with even more archaic elements: 78rpm recordings of early French music hall gear that Roméo appears to scratch as it plays. 

Crucial listening FFO Jan Jelinek, Andrew Pekler, or the Gallic end of the Finders Keepers reissue programme.

items.body:
Dead strong etheric elisions of chamber-jazz, trip hop and dream-pop from Bristol’s Tara Clerkin Trio, following up their acclaimed self-titled debut with a new EP of subdued but glowing reveries somewhere between Dominique Lawalrée's intimate parlour music, Third Eye Foundation's atmospheric configurations and the sort of skewed pop we'll always associate with the Laika x Moonshake axis. 

The effortless drift of ’In Spring’ is the trio’s 2nd vinyl release after 2019’s eponymous debut and a tape with Dublin’s Weeding in 2020. It’s a distinctly Bristolian affair in its beatdown pacing and smoky atmosphere, which the label themselves compare to the roster orbiting the city’s Planet Records (Flying Saucer Attack, The Third Eye Foundation) in the ‘90s, with hints of a less noirish Portishead, or the sweeter ends of the Young Echo sound.

'Memory' dissolves into the atmosphere, all muted woodwind and organ moans that erupt into a half-time drum warble; if trip-hop is back in 2021, "In Spring" recalls the genre's most low-key and thus enduring moments, while harmonizing with the wyrd-world narco-pop abstraction of contemporary forces Cucina Povera and Leila Sakini. 

Their elegant chamber sashay ‘Done Before’ carries Tara’s vocals on beautifully buoyant string and piano phrases trimmed with a sort of tripped sensibility, and ‘Night Steps’ pushes that aspect with crushed drums and filtered vox that feel like Teresa Winter on a Portishead track, and their nuanced range finally reaches into a sort of modal, 4th world lounge style recalling Julia Holter via Air on the impessively accomplished title tune. 

A quietly brilliant, memorable record >> Tipped!

items.body:
Effortlessly easy on the ear and yet still somehow fathoms-deep, Tara Clerkin Trio’s latest is their most refined and fully-formed transmission yet, mining a precious sweetspot between chamber-jazz, Plone-style bric-a-brac electronics, Crescent’s lo-fi reveries and the urban pressure of the Young Echo collective, unpicking decades of British musical history in the process. Trust, it’s a special one.

Like every great band, TCT know their history. They've grown up with and formed their identity in the shadow of Bristol's musical lore, whether it's The Pop Group, Massive Attack or Flying Saucer Attack, and when they use traceable elements, it feels like a believable part of their DNA. Thankfully, they meaningfully add to that narrative too, not adapting an aesthetic for easy consumption. Part of this might be down to their makeup; they formed in the late 20-teens from the ashes of the Tara Clerkin Band, a larger ensemble that Clerkin had put together to expand the scope of her folk-y pop compositions. And when most of the members moved on, stepbrothers Sunny-Joe Paradiso and Patrick Benjamin stuck around to see where the road might lead. All "proper" players, they've traditionally let their songs appear from what sounds like loose, casual improvisations, like you're tuned into Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society' band running through Laika's 'Silver Apples of the Moon'.

So you get a song like the brilliant 'Ups & Downs', that simmers for a good four minutes with wheezing harmonium, double bass and clarinet, percussion just rumbling in the background somewhere, before a jerky sampled beat, Mellotron strings and Clerkin's voice would have you thinking Matt Elliott's behind the boards. But 'Somewhere Good' is also remarkably tight when it needs to be, walking a tightrope between easy breezy and meticulous with acrobatic skill. Opener 'Lake Walk', for example, sounds intentionally naive, jammed out loosely on synthesised and real woodwind that's caught in a vortex of Space Echo, before 'Lazy Daisy' cuts it short with its more ordered (but still kinda slouchy) beat-heavy dreampop atmosphere. It's where the album's shape really coagulates, between Broadcast's dramatic early EPs (back when they were touring with Plone) and Pram's best shit, just lightly tweezed at the edges, its creases relaxed to fit in with Laila Sakini's quietly genius 'Paloma'. And that mood carries the record even when Clerkin's voice - pursed into a soulful croon or a lackadaisical murmur - vanishes completely. One of the most gripping moments arrives with 'There Was a Nice Sunset', effortlessly matching slowcore drums with piano flourishes and synths, locking into the same general feeling but widening the boundaries, nodding to Adrian Sherwood's lysergic work on Creation Rebel's 'Starship Africa'. 

There's years of British musical history baked into this stuff, and yet it feels wholly new.

The precocious, recombinant jazz talents of a 22 year old Michael Gregory Jackson, and pals, are beautifully captured on his 1977 debut, yielding early shoots of his pop ambitions in Jacquardian weaves of jazz-fusion, neo-classical and flamenco, with unique appeal.

Stemming from mid ‘70s free jazz roots with empathic players, Oliver Lake, David Murray & Wadada Leo Smith, a young Jackson beautifully took the lead on debut album ‘Clarity’ with a mix of advanced musicality and naïf wanderlust yielding singular results. Shifting with a striking elegance beyond his years, from free jazz to ballads, flamenco and sinuous, angular neoclassical minimalism, the album remains a strangely calming yet quizzical curio in its field, yet wholly characteristic of developments in jazz at the time. 50 years after the fact, it’s hard not to be enamoured with its ambitious scope and reserved discipline.

The titular opening gambit is a total gem, initially smudging distinctions of jazz and chamber classical, before a gorgeous R&B soul vocal lands from above, and you just know it’s going to get special. Funnily enough, that voice doesn’t appear again for the rest of the album, but that quite alright as the instrumentalists pucker and stretch out with a mix of vividly lyrical and conversational qualities, even in a ‘Ballad’ whose title would surely imply a voice in there somewhere. From a pastoral gem ‘A View of This Life’ recalling aspects of Luciano Cilio, thru quietly breathtaking take on classical flamenco in ‘Prelueoionti’ foreshadowing Jim O’Rourke tekkerz, to almost Stockhausen-esque angularity in ‘CLARITY 4’, and its sublime closer ‘IOMI’, it’s deeply impressive stuff.

TIP!

items.body:
Skullflower’s band-mind ’92 noise rock salvo for JK Broadrick’s label is back to infect the water table on its 30th anniversary repress, newly augmented with a 2nd disc of extra, unreleased cuts from the same recording sessions - prime, atonal gnarl for disciples of Godflesh, Broken Flag, Fushitsusha

Originally recorded in London, 1991, and released on Justin “Godflesh” Broadrick’s hEADdIRt in ’92, ‘IIIrd Gatekeeper’ marks the point when Matthew Bower (guitar), Anthony Di Franco (bass) and Stuart Dennison’s (drums, vocals) Skullflower were three years deep into their thing, and hailed among the world’s heaviest guitar bands. Issued against a backdrop of peak grunge, the album sees Skullflower continue to take their cues from the UK’s noise and power-electronics scene with little compromise, resulting a genre-defining, cataclysmic event whose nuclear fallout would feed forward to inspire everyone from Godflesh to Khanate, Sunn 0))) and Blackhaine. 

Surely worthy of Sunn 0)))’s maxim, that “maximum volume yields maximum effect”, this is one to be played a neighbour-harassing levels. On the LP’s original eight tracks they lay waste to sears and amps with the sheer, overdriven, sludgy force of ‘Can You Feel It?’, the thrumming motorik momentum of ‘Black Rabbit’ and ‘Godzilla’, or Di Franco’s thunderous bass on ‘Larks Tongue’, and the rope-end howl of ’Spoiler’. The bonus disc now gets behind the studio curtain to spy them resembling O.L.D. on the synth streaked alien noise rock of ‘Stars and Bars’, beside the elephantine swagger of ‘Wand’, and a lurching ’Evil Twin’ that should all be enough to warrant old heads updating battered copies, and likely to sever the heads of new lambs to their slaughter.

A shining star in Mika Vainio’s dense microcosm returns to vinyl - and for our money it’s the most transcendent record in his revered catalogue, unfurling through an hour of disarmingly melodic romance and astral projection that never fails to bring a tear to our eye.

First presented on CD in 2005 under Vainio’s Ø alias, ‘Kantamoinen’ became something of a sleeper gem, cultishly adored for its concerted embrace of extended melody and narrative tone within an ambient context, which made it stand out from his preceding decade of ascetic noise brutalism and minimal techno. 

Our first encounter, back at our Pelicanneck shop, left us utterly smitten with its soundtrack-like qualities, eventually prompting us to issue it on vinyl for the first time via our Editions label in 2016. Sadly, Mika passed the following year, which only made the material more precious as a lone, curious artefact in his deeply influential body of work. It now returns in this new edition, ready to flip preconceptions with a new generation of listeners through its exquisite carousel of tear-jerking soundscpaes where the artist’s most intimate, distinctive spirits endure.

Dedicated to Mika’s grandma, Laina Vainio (1913-1991), and adorned with a cover image of her garden in Artjärvi, Finland, the 16-part 2LP is the closest you’ll get to a type of nostalgia in Mika’s catalogue. Whilst recorded 1999-2004 at an early crest of his game-changing work with Pan Sonic, the album clearly manifests a quieter space for Mika to emote far more nuanced feels, from the wide-eyed vastness of ‘Galaxy’ to a breathtaking ‘Sound Picture’, transitioning from Hans-Ulrich Obrist’s snippet of Oskar Sala into icy bliss, and the rosy warmth of a ‘Summerland’ clearly dedicated to his nan’s garden. 

The rest is better defined as ephemeral snapshots adding up to a broader picture, like a mind’s eye filling gaps in the memory from illusive vapours and sensations, generating all-time gems in the steepled choral synth voice of ‘In Wind’, or a sense of magic realism in the swaying organ of ‘Antenna-ant’, with the blooz folk wheeze of closer ‘To Home’ that could feasibly score the most haunting moments of a Bela Tarr flick.

A wondrous, wonderful record.

items.body:
Magnum opus-weight album from organist and electro-acoustic composer Anna von Hausswolff, the entire record consists of just one instrument - the pipe organ, and represents absolute liberation of the imagination. It's a masterwork of gothic classical beauty - a must check for fans of Kali Malone, Kara-Lis Coverdale.

‘All Thoughts Fly’ was recorded at Gothenburg’s Örgryte New Church  and is heavily infused with the space’s atmospheric nuance, which renders the theatric richness of Anna’s compositions at their most billowing and melodramatic. As her 6th album, it’s also her most confident and strikingly original, following the slow steady procession of her sides for Kning Disk, Touch and City Slang with her most sepulchral and steepled refinement of black metal atmospheres and sacred dirges pronounced with an apocalyptic classical grandeur and iconoclastic experimental daring.

“Notes on the recording process: The organ on All Thoughts Fly is situated in Gothenburg and is a Swedish replica of the Arp Schnitger organ in Germany. It is the largest organ tuned in Quarter-comma meantone temperament in the world. With it’s four manuals, one pedal and 54 stops, it was built as part of a ten-year research project reconstructing 17th Century North German organ building craft. The tuning temperament is an important detail to note here, as it deeply affects the sound and tuning, and thus radically changed the process of creating this album. Anna speaks of a pleasant surprise during recording, the organ's ability to create beautiful "pitching" notes through its stops and air supply system. She remarks “We took advantage of this so most of the pitching sounds and notes that you hear on the album comes from the mechanics of this organ, effects made entirely acoustically." The organ was recorded with two room mics for atmosphere and two pairs of close mics placed inside the organ to capture nuances and detail for further organ sound processing by Filip Leyman in his studio.”

Someone had to do it: Ennio Morricone and co.’s creepy OST for Pier Paolo Pasolini’s scandalous ’75 film rendition of the notorious novel ‘120 Days of Sodom’, by Marquis De Sade, lands on arch industrialist label, Cold Spring. Mangia!

Next in the label’s line of cult scores, after ‘Decoder’ and Psychic TV’s ‘A Prayer for Derek Jarman’, comes this deeply uneasy score to Pasolini’s infamous enactment of De Sade’s pornographic dystopia-come-study of male power dynamics. Whether you’ve seen it or not, the book and film’s reputation precedes them as both a piece of pure, unadulterated filth, or handy encyclopaedia of depravity, depending on one’s take. Each to their own, as one might say, but fuck me: without going into snuff or dark web realms, the imagery is about as mad as it gets. Which all makes the soundtrack of breezy to discordant chamber classical (Bach, Chopin, Orff, Puccini, and Graziosi) and parlour jazz arrangements register even harder in the memory, especially when paired with its scenes representing everything from coprophilia to bestiality, incest, and worse.

items.body:
Veteran Dutch sound artist, engineer and composer Jos Smolders teams up with Jim O'Rourke for the second time on 'Albumin', following up their low-key electroacoustic LP 'Additive Inverse' with another full set of fluctuating Kyma textures, cybernetic granulations and oddball spectralisations. Deep, dank material, tipped FFO Roland Kayn, Nurse With Wound, Kevin Drumm.

It took O'Rourke and Smolders three years to assemble 'Albumin', going back and forth with day-long sessions that each artist worked into independently, shuttling the results over to the other side of the world. The methodology was roughly the same as it was for 2021's 'Additive Inverse', except this time O'Rourke instigated the process, sending Smolders a bounty of material that established the original sound. And while you'll be familiar with O'Rourke's Kyma processes if you've spent any amount of time investigating his Steamroom catlog, Smolders' subtle rhythmic elements put 'Albumin' in its own category. 

Opening side '(HP-HP)' plays like a fully self-contained album all on its own, beginning with industrial sounds and cybernetic groans that buckle and break under their own pressure, cutting into batshit electroacoustic rhythms that might as well have been snatched from an early GRM reel. Soon, the creaky strings and oscillations are expertly fashioned into subterranean resonances that Smolders and O'Rourke treat with music box-cum-gamelan twinkles. What makes it so startling is the fact that it's never completely obvious what it is we're hearing, exactly. There's a smudge of vaseline over every surface that gives it an unearthly shimmer; even if the sounds start off in tangible spaces.

On the flip, the duo continue down the same crooked path, blurring the line between fantasy and reality. Ornate film score strings are ruptured by glitches before the duo stretch them into unstable, warbling drones. Listen closely and you can still just about hear the base orchestral characteristics, but the duo's aggy outbursts of synthesized rhythm and ear-splitting feedback keep tearing the material at its far edges, making sure the dream never gets too placid.

It's nail-biting stuff; heard at low volume it's almost an illusion, with insectoid sounds batting against a backdrop of hums and groans, but crank it up and you'll discover an entire ecosystem.

items.body:
Toronto-based brothers Kevin and Patrick Cahill return to Death Is Not The End with another set of introspective folk-inspired instrumentals.

They might play nylon strung guitar and make what's in all respects "folk" music, but East of the Valley Blues don't draw from the expected sources, balancing out their interest in Americana with an understanding of music from across the world that genuinely widens their perspective. So their percussive opener 'Sitting in the Poem' can swerve utterly fluidly from serpentine Tuareg-inspired riffage to Fahey-esque fingerstyle and you barely notice it. And 'The Spider Underneath' can sound utterly outside the timeline, playing like an extended post-rock jam recorded in a basement in North Africa.

Taking one side of the stereo spectrum each, the brothers play off each other perfectly, leaving us to fill in the gaps. And they peak on the brilliant 'Like Fitzcarraldo', seemingly blending South American styles and plodding rock - no need to tug a steamboat over a mountain though, right? Or play Enrico Caruso in the Amazon.

Rami Abadir rejects lazy futurism on his Planet Mu debut, instead studying the Arab world's historic rhythms, instruments and techniques and using that raw material to galvanize a suite of contemporary club music that sails far beyond the usual 4/4 template. It's dynamic, charismatic gear - crucial dancer's biz FFO Toumba, 3Phaz, Siete Catorce and Slikback.

Like us, Abadir has noticed that the now-ubiquitous dystopian club fantasy has become a self-fulfilling prophecy in the last few years. What started as a subversive examination of the cultural status quo from radical non-white voices like Nkisi and Chino Amobi was swiftly co-opted by a well-heeled Eurocentric elite who traded any empathy for naive-but-marketable indifference. So on 'The Primitivist' he addresses the situation directly, following his hybridized SVBKVLT breakout 'Mutate' with another dancefloor-ready suite that sources its ingredients closer to home. Where its predecessor looked for nexus points between the Maqsoum rhythm and reggaeton or jungle, 'The Primitivist' locks into the Arab region, reaching from Egypt to Iraq, Kuwait, Syria and Palestine and adapting traditional elements with bold modern techniques. 

The best point of comparison might be the "Tribal Prehispánico" concept proposed by early N.A.A.F.I. legend Javier Estrada, who re-imagined Mexico's tribal guarachero sound using even more fundamental local instrumentation and advanced DAW knowledge. Abadir's music is still functionally modern, sharpened with the techniques he's refined over years of performing in some of the world's most notorious clubs and festival spaces, but it's been shaped by history - he doesn't attempt to bury his head in the sand as drones barrage the dunes surrounding him. On 'Habban', Abadir engages in his own kind of sonic warfare, disrupting a 4/4 pulse with Iraqi khishba drum samples, darbuka rhythms and reshaping the melodic content using synthesized buzuq-style pentatonic riffs. And the title track takes the concept even further, shoehorning live syncopated hand drum rhythms into a progression of glossed builds and drops that hits its crescendo with the shrill wail of Levantine mijwiz reed pipes.

Elsewhere, Abadir adapts the 8-beat tsifteteli rhythm - a staple at Greek and Turkish weddings - on 'Pass & Go', chopping it with abrupt interjections and breakneck rolls and heads back home on 'This is Not Another Maqsoum', spiking the Egyptian pattern with elements cribbed from the Bedouin al-Dahiyya folk dance. It's some of the best club music (or wedding music, actually) you're likely to hear this year.

items.body:
Copenhagen’s meme-able, custom line of genre-blurring songwriters yields Lithuanian talent, Gintè Preisait, fresh from the conservatoire and an LP with Toshimaru Nakamura, on an enchanted, waking dream blend of lower case concrète, trip hop and avant-classical experimentation calling to mind the refined crafts of ML Buch, Ugné Uma, Svitlana Nianio, Smerz, Lucrecia Dalt, Julia Holter or Martyna Basta, thru the reaches of Finland’s Fonal Records.

It was bound to happen at some point, right? We've written more than enough about how Copenhagen's Rhythmic Music Conservatory has become the central node in a scene that's prioritized the permeable membrane between pop, classical training and unhinged technological experimentation - honestly where else are you gonna find Clarissa Connelly, Astrid Sonne, Erika de Casier, ML Buch and Fine? Gintė Preisaitė pushes even further into uncharted waters on her debut album, letting the pop forms evaporate like vapors around her intricately woven experimental collages. We're already off to a good start with 'Vigilance', a lengthy introduction that pays its respects to Preisaitė's past, present and future. The classically trained improviser, producer and composer begins with an ensemble of moaning acoustic instruments that she gradually chips into, tearing through the acoustic sounds with electronic treatments and introducing subtle, grounding field recordings before adding her voice and completely shifting the direction. 

The unwieldy blend of elements prepares us for an arguably bolder experiment, 'Summary Saint Mary', where Preisaitė matches her gamelan-like prepared piano phrases with Björk-ish vocal loops, OPN-inspired electronic touches and wheezing processed acoustic sounds. And it's remarkably well controlled; even in capable hands, it's a tough palette to work with and Preisaitė makes it look almost easy, never stepping too far in any direction or another. Because it's not really a pop record at all, it's an album that's aware of pop, doesn't avoid its charms, but manages to corral its characteristics into the avant garde's misshapen spirit. Even the relatively upbeat, straightforward 'Aéroport', a track that would have sounded stylistically comfortable on Smerz's RMC love-in 'Big city life EDITS', she never goes full James K, letting the melodies curve towards freeform abstraction in the final act before hitting us with three tracks of choppy, half-dissolved prepared piano. It's ambitious stuff, and all the better for it.

Deep club modernist Sa Pa mints his own new label, Dub Techno For Life, with four top drawer cuts of textured, strident pressure tipped FFO classic Chain Reaction x Short Span.

Since 2015 Sa Pa has carved a heads-down path between techno, proper, and its conceptual adjuncts in ambient and sound designer atmospheres, most recently on Short Span and Astral Industries. Now taking matters into his own hands, the ‘Girls on Tour EP’ squares up his most robust club material alongside more experimental urges for a definitive self-portrait displaying a fine spectrum of strengths. 

The four tunes clearly speak to his diversity within a theme, checking for a firm touchstone in Andreas Tilliander aka Mokira with the 10 mins of rolling, claggy heft to ‘Mokira Ultra Dub’, unshelving his 2016 rework for deep ’26 ‘floors, alongside the puckered elegance of ‘Waiting For You’, harking to roots in Teutonic house minimalism, whereas the B-side attends to grubbier urges in the bittersweet, sludgy budge of ‘Modular System’, and lusher, abstract feels on the Actress or Rezzett-esque whorl of ‘World Saving Banger’.

A mini-album from "language contortionist" Anastasia Freygang and Japanese pop shapeshifter Koichi Yamanoha (aka Grimm Grimm), 'Yamaha Dogs' is electronic music as performance art.

What can you really say about a record when its 'Intro' is the second track? LISA take surrealism to its limit on 'Yamaha Dogs', not so much writing songs but dissolving musical remnants on the fly as if they're performing an upsetting stage show, with clowns. On the anxiety-inducing 'Anus Sun', Freygang's groans and repetitions machinegun over Yamanoha's cheap electronic drum hits and it's hard to tell which is more disconcerting. And on the accurately monikered 'No Dance', a 4/4 thud is disrupted by off-grid clicks, Hank Shocklee-style horn samples and bitcrushed, overloaded computer meltdown sounds that transform into screams. Nowt else quite like it.

items.body:
Andrew Field-Pickering (aka Max D) and Matt Papich (aka Co La) consider the process of filmmaking on their fifth album, adding foley sounds and concrète elements to their improvised jazz, dub and post-rock soundscapes, bringing in more eaze, Future Times' Mezey, Motion Graphics, bagpipeer Duncan S. Moore and Ponytail's Dustin Wong and Jeremy Hyman as additional castmembers. 

Their last proper album, 'Trellis', arrived on Peak Oil following a run of deployments for PAN and Max D's own Future Times imprint and appeared to take stock of their run until that point, a surreal collage of studio recordings with input from a few trusted collaborators - all of whom appear on 'Movie'. But this new set feels more like a line in the sand, a statement record that focuses the core duo's skills around a loose concept: cinema. And that's not even to say the album is explicitly filmic in any particular way; Lifted don't make music that's supposed to be absorbed as a soundtrack as such, or seen as being inspired by any particular composers, either. It's driven by their experiences with film over the years, their deep, cinephile (not film bro) understanding of the filmmaking methodology. Robert Altman's pioneering use of overlapping dialog, for instance, a technique that had barely been heard before 'M*A*S*H', or the lavish, multi-track recording style that helped bring 'Nashville' to life. They also reference Thai "slow cinema" maestro Apichatpong Weerasethakul, whose ability to focus on seemingly insignificant sounds - just check 'Memoria' and thank us later - has inspired Lifted's process for years.

'The Ice Chewers' acts as their title card and Field-Pickering and Papich put the prolific more eaze to good use immediately, backing up her bass guitar, pedal steel and acoustic guitar parts with their usual CDJ trickery and arsenal of FX techniques and brilliantly broken up live drums. Using tape stop effects to pitch the material as if they're putting their thumb on the master, the duo sound as if they're tinkering with the reel, burning it out just like Ingmar Bergman did in 'Persona' to remind you it was all celluloid. Musically, it's a throwback to Tortoise's enduring 'TNT', that Lifted use like a teaser, letting it dissolve completely before hitting us with the noir-ish 'Paranoids'. Here, harsh foley sounds overlap with indistinct dialog and environmental echoes that the duo loop and echo, painting an indistinct picture of a film that might be as eerie as 'The Conversation' or as eroticized as 'Klute'. Their work with voices is particularly impressive; film samples in music are so overdone but it all sounds fresh here - mostly thanks to their attention to Altman-esque detail.

On 'Repossessed' they shift into chillier territory and nattily avoid the churned Carpenterisms that have held synth music back this last decade. Instead, Lifted focus on echo, twisting the emphasis on an amateurish piano improv from Papich to suggest that there's something moving in the distance. Of course, it all makes their VHS gore-inspired 'Melts Very Nasty' hit much harder; again, they don't go the obvious route and try to recreate the 'Street Trash' soundtrack, they hint at the general aura, using grotesque sound effects, Mezey and Motion Graphics' submerged synths and Moore's bagpipes to show and not tell. They even hold back a genuine belter for the end credits: the soft rock-inspired 'Midnight Snack'.

Even if you think you've got a lid on Lifted, 'Movie' really takes things to the next level.

items.body:
Egyptian trio The Handover crystallise farther Arabic jams for oud, violin, and synth on Sublime Frequencies, reprising the mesmerising appeal of their shows, as on 2024’s self-titled side, and one we caught as Islington Mill, Salford, where Graham Massey was cooing over their rare vintage keyboard…

“Hot on the heals of their spectacular self-titled debut album, The Handover is back with their second long form composition, New Old Medicine. Aly Eissa (oud), Ayman Asfour (violin), and Jonas Cambien (vintage organ/synth) have been cutting their teeth on the international touring circuit for the past two years, landing from town to town in their seductive spaceship to blow people's minds and then dematerialize into the void. An outline for a new piece began to emerge along the route and late last year during a stop in Berlin, this metamorphosis of the trio's sound was recorded in pristine form by Rabih Beaini at Morphine Studios.

Attempting to define the music is not as important as allowing it to define itself - from person to person, village to village. All we can do is suggest what may resonate to lure you into the arena; psychedelic, folkloric, Egyptian, etc., as these excerpts from the liner notes suggest: "Though one long piece, New Old Medicine moves through several unofficial chapters. It originates in the psychic depths with a pensive melody. Gradually solidifying, the organ’s first solo ushers the piece into a swaying, reverent dance. This dance nears its end with a vigorously percussive section on oud, handing it off to the violin for a climactic solo. A momentary pause, then the rhythm thickens, and the musicians ride untethered through the midnight. This frenzy is followed by a calm repose on placid water. But this calm is merely a deep inhale before the final charged ascent into cosmic rapture."

Tokyo-based artist Ayami Suzuki remembers her father on 'Remnants', considering the traces that loved ones leave when they die by blurring her musical elements into indistinct but emotional clouds of ambient sound. RIYL William Basinski, Celer or Lawrence English.

Who said mourning needed to be solemn? 'Remnants' is an album about grief, in a way, but it's also about presence itself - the pieces of a person that are left after they're gone. Interpreting that in sound isn't easy, so Suzuki stays relatively abstract, hiding her intentions behind droning, harmonic clouds, melancholy breaths that sound as if they're trapped behind layers of noise. It's nothing particularly novel, but it's affecting all the same, especially if you listen while studying the cover.

items.body:
Berlin-based Argentinian composer Ángeles Rojas plays pipe organ on this one, backed by a small ensemble who mimic her sustained tones and discreet variations. RIYL Kali Malone, Ellen Arkbro et al.

You're probably sick of the pipe organ by now, but Rojas is at least approaching it with a little spice. Commissioned by Argentina's RUIDO festival, 'Open the Windows and Let the Spirits in and Out' was recorded at Buenos Aires' National Auditorium/CCK, a huge symphony hall that houses a Klaie Opus 1912 organ. And Rojas wrote the piece specifically for the instrument, noting its distinct character and picking an ensemble that would complement it. She writes for violin, cello, flute, saxophone, trombone and clarinet, and these additional instruments are subtly introduced, breathing alongside a drone that moves so slowly it seems to be completely static. Of course, there's more happening than meets the ear at first - Rojas' oh-so-tiny variations are enhanced subtly by each instrument. Heard in the background it won't make sense at all, listened to closely everything falls into place.
